title: Narrative Techniques & Storytelling
description: How stories work — point of view, structure, characterisation, setting, pacing, tension, and narrative voice.

notes.heading: Point of View (POV)
notes.body: First person ('I/me'): intimate, subjective — reader experiences events through one character's eyes. Unreliable narrator: first-person narrator who misleads readers (intentionally or not) — creates dramatic irony and demands critical reading. Second person ('you'): rare — directly addresses reader. Creates immediacy, used in choose-your-own-adventure and some literary fiction. Third person limited: follows ONE character's thoughts/feelings — 'he thought,' 'she felt.' More objective than first person but still filtered. Third person omniscient: all-knowing narrator can describe any character's thoughts and feelings, move freely through time and space. POV shapes everything: what reader knows, whose perspective is privileged, how much trust we place in narration.

notes.heading: Narrative Structure
notes.body: Classic Freytag's Pyramid: Exposition (characters, setting, situation introduced) → Rising action (conflicts develop, complications arise) → Climax (moment of highest tension, turning point) → Falling action (consequences unfold) → Resolution/Dénouement (conflicts resolved or deliberately left open). Non-linear structures: In medias res — starting in the middle of action, then revealing backstory. Frame narrative — a story within a story (Wuthering Heights, Frankenstein). Reverse chronology — told backwards. Circular narrative — ends where it begins. Episodic — separate stories linked by theme/character. Modern and postmodern works often deliberately disrupt conventional structure.

notes.heading: Foreshadowing, Flashback and Pacing
notes.body: Foreshadowing: hints planted early about later events. Can be subtle (symbolic imagery) or direct (prophecy). Creates anticipation and reread value. Flashback (analepsis): interrupts present to show past events — reveals backstory, motivation, or hidden information. Flash-forward (prolepsis): glimpses the future. Pacing: how quickly events unfold. Short sentences, rapid scene changes, and action sequences accelerate pacing. Long descriptive passages, internal monologue, and detailed setting slow pacing. Authors vary pacing to control tension and emphasise moments. Tension: created through conflict (internal/external), stakes (what's at risk), uncertainty (what might happen), and timing (delayed resolution).

notes.heading: Characterisation: Direct and Indirect
notes.body: Direct characterisation: narrator explicitly describes character traits. 'She was a kind and patient woman.' Indirect characterisation: reveals character through — Speech (what they say, how they say it), Thoughts (internal monologue), Effect on others (how other characters react), Actions (what they do), Looks (appearance, clothing, body language). Mnemonic: STEAL. Round characters: complex, develop over time, have internal conflicts. Flat characters: one-dimensional, serve a specific function. Dynamic characters: undergo significant change. Static characters: remain unchanged. Foils: secondary characters whose contrast highlights protagonist's qualities.

notes.heading: Setting and Atmosphere
notes.body: Setting: time AND place of the narrative — historical period, geographical location, time of day, season, weather, social environment. Functions of setting: establishes mood/atmosphere, reflects characters' emotional states (pathetic fallacy), creates conflict/obstacles, symbolises themes, provides context. Atmosphere: the emotional tone pervading a scene — created through sensory details, word choice (diction), pacing, and imagery. Gothic atmosphere: darkness, decay, isolation, supernatural. Dystopian atmosphere: oppression, surveillance, despair, greyness. Setting is NOT neutral background — it actively shapes meaning. Ask: how would the story change if set elsewhere/when else?

notes.heading: Dialogue and Voice
notes.body: Dialogue reveals character, advances plot, creates tension, and provides exposition (but avoid 'As you know, Bob...' — forced exposition). Good dialogue: sounds natural but is more purposeful than real speech, reveals subtext (what characters DON'T say), reflects character background/education/emotion, uses interruptions and silences. Dialogue tags: 'said' is usually best (invisible to reader). Overuse of alternatives ('exclaimed,' 'retorted,' 'opined') distracts. Vernacular/dialect: can establish authenticity and character, but avoid caricature. Internal monologue: reveals character's unspoken thoughts — creates intimacy between reader and character. Stream of consciousness: captures the chaotic, associative flow of thought.

notes.heading: Theme and Symbolism
notes.body: Theme: the central idea or message — what the story is really about beyond the plot. NOT a single word ('love') but a statement ('love can be both destructive and redemptive'). Stories can have multiple themes. Symbolism: concrete objects, characters, or events representing abstract ideas. A rose may symbolise love, a storm turmoil, a journey self-discovery. Symbols can be universal (cultural) or contextual (created within the work). Motif: a recurring element (image, phrase, situation) that reinforces theme. Identifying theme: (1) What does the protagonist learn? (2) What conflicts recur? (3) What is the title's significance? (4) How does the ending comment on the beginning?

flashcards.definition: Uses 'I/me.' Reader experiences events through one character's subjective perspective.
flashcards.example: 'I walked into the dark room, my heart pounding.' Unreliable if narrator misleads.

flashcards.definition: All-knowing — can describe any character's thoughts/feelings, move freely in time/space.
Moment of highest tension — the turning point where the central conflict peaks.
Hints planted early about events to come. Creates anticipation and depth.
flashcards.example: A Dark storm approaching as hero sets out on a dangerous journey.

flashcards.definition: Interruption of present to show past events — reveals backstory or motivation.
Starting the story in the middle of action, then revealing earlier events later.
Revealing character through Speech, Thoughts, Effect on others, Actions, Looks.
flashcards.example: Character slams door, refuses to eat (actions) → angry, without narrator stating it.

flashcards.definition: Nature/weather reflecting characters' emotions. A narrative technique linking setting to mood.
flashcards.example: Rain during a funeral. Sunshine at a wedding. Thunder during a confrontation.

flashcards.definition: Central idea/message — what the story is really about beyond the plot. A statement, not a word.
Concrete object/character/event representing an abstract idea.
flashcards.example: Green light in Gatsby = unattainable dreams. Conch in Lord of the Flies = civilisation/order.

flashcards.definition: First-person narrator who misleads/distorts — readers must critically evaluate their account.
flashcards.example: Holden Caulfield (Catcher in the Rye) — his judgments may not reflect reality.

flashcards.definition: A recurring element (image, phrase, situation) throughout a work that reinforces theme.
flashcards.example: Blood motif in Macbeth — recurring references to blood symbolise guilt that cannot be washed away.
